title: Views of self (section 31)
hook: views of self and being are not views; so they are called views

segments.voice: Yesterday, dust and worlds: a world ground to specks, and neither world nor dust a fixed thing. Your line: a world of dust. Which solid block did you break into pieces? Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

Two friends walk out of a movie. One says, that was brilliant. The other says, that was a mess. By the time they reach the parking lot, it's no longer about the movie. Each one is defending something closer to home: my taste, my judgment, me. A view started as a way of seeing a film and became a wall to stand behind. Section thirty-one of the Diamond Sutra goes after the view that sits underneath all the others, the view of a self. And, true to form, it doesn't swap it for a better view. It does something quieter. Today: views of self.
screen: `BRILLIANT. A MESS.` → `NOT ABOUT THE MOVIE NOW.` → `THE VIEW UNDER THE VIEWS.`

segments.voice: First, the question. The Buddha asks Subhuti, in paraphrase: if someone said the Tathagata taught a view of a self, a view of a being, a view of a living soul, a view of a person, would they be speaking rightly? No, says Subhuti. Second, the answer's shape. What the Tathagata taught as a view of self, Subhuti says, is taught as no view, and that is why it's called a view of self. The same four ideas the sutra has cut since its opening sections come back one last time, and this time it isn't the self being cut. It's the view of it. Third, where that leaves the bodhisattva. The Buddha says that one who sets out on this path should know all things, see all things, and trust all things in such a way that they don't hold on to even an idea of a thing. And then, of course: an idea of a thing is no idea; that's why it's called an idea. Even the sutra's own teaching about no self is not a new belief to clutch. Fourth, the week. Look at what this one cut. No beings freed: help without the ledger. Form and sound: not the face or the voice. Not annihilation: and still, not nothing. Merit not held. Neither coming nor going. Dust and worlds. And now views of self. Every day the blade has had the same edge. It doesn't throw away beings, bodies, merit or worlds. It takes away the grip. Today it reaches a deeper grip: the grip on being right about who we are.
screen: `DID HE TEACH A VIEW OF SELF?` · `NO VIEW, SO CALLED A VIEW.` · `NOT EVEN AN IDEA OF A THING.` · `THE WEEK: THE GRIP, NOT THE THING.` · then, large: `SO-CALLED VIEWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: hold one view lightly. Settle, and breathe. Bring up one opinion you hold firmly, about a person, a habit, a team, or about yourself. Let it sit in your mind the way a stone sits in an open palm. Notice where it presses: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Don't drop it, and don't argue with it. Just loosen the fingers. It's a view. It's called a view. Let the breath move around it. The bell holds the time.
Views of self. Section thirty-one: what the Tathagata taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and so it's called a view. Today's word.
Your line: so-called views. Today, when you catch yourself defending an opinion, add the words so called under your breath, and see if the grip eases. Day one thousand one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Mahayana teachers read section 31 of the Diamond Sutra as a warning not to turn the teaching of no self into one more view to defend; students meet it in chanting, study and meditation on how views are held.

fork.setup: you're Subhuti. someone says the Tathagata taught a view of self, of a being, of a soul, of a person. are they right?
options: no: a view of self is taught as no view
partly: he taught only the view of a person
fork.reveal: Subhuti says no: what was taught as a view of self is taught as no view, and that's why it's called a view of self.

original.note: Sanskrit (Pali ditthi): a view, a way of seeing; in section 31, the 'view of self' that is no view.

trapdoor: what you thought: Buddhism replaces 'I have a self' with 'I have no self.'
what it means: the sutra won't let either become a view to clutch; even the idea of a thing is 'so called.'
what a scholar hears: section 31 moves from the four ideas of self, being, soul and person to the views of them, and ends on not holding even an idea of a dharma.
